function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
**Java** is a high‑level, class‑based, object‑oriented programming language that was originally developed by James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle Corporation). It was first released in 1995 as part of the Sun Microsystems Java platform.

---

## Core Characteristics

| Feature | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Platform‑independent** | Java code is compiled into *bytecode* that runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). The same bytecode works on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and many other systems without modification. |
| **Object‑oriented** | Everything is an object (except primitives). Inheritance, encapsulation, polymorphism, and abstraction are first‑class concepts. |
| **Strongly typed** | Variables must be declared with a type, and type checking happens at compile time. |
| **Automatic memory management** | Garbage collection automatically frees memory that is no longer referenced. |
| **Rich standard library** | The Java Standard Edition (SE) includes APIs for collections, networking, I/O, concurrency, GUI (Swing, JavaFX), and more. |
| **Security** | The JVM sandbox, bytecode verification, and security manager help protect against malicious code. |
| **Multithreading** | Built‑in support for concurrent execution via the `java.lang.Thread` class and higher‑level concurrency utilities (`java.util.concurrent`). |

---

## Typical Use Cases

| Domain | Why Java is popular |
|--------|---------------------|
| **Enterprise applications** | Robust, scalable, and supported by mature frameworks (Spring, Jakarta EE). |
| **Android apps** | Android’s native language (until Kotlin became the preferred choice) is Java. |
| **Web servers & microservices** | High performance, strong typing, and extensive ecosystem (Spring Boot, Micronaut). |
| **Big data & analytics** | Hadoop, Spark, and other big‑data tools are written in Java or provide Java APIs. |
| **Embedded systems** | Java ME (Micro Edition) and Java SE Embedded target resource‑constrained devices. |
| **Desktop GUIs** | Swing, JavaFX, and third‑party libraries enable cross‑platform desktop apps. |

---

## Quick Example

```java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, world!");
    }
}
```

Compile and run:

```bash
javac HelloWorld.java   # compiles to HelloWorld.class (bytecode)
java HelloWorld         # JVM executes the bytecode
```

---

## Java vs. JavaScript

| Aspect | Java | JavaScript |
|--------|------|------------|
| Origin | 1995, Sun Microsystems | 1995, Netscape |
| Syntax | C‑style, statically typed | C‑style, dynamically typed |
| Runtime | JVM (bytecode) | Browser engine / Node.js |
| Primary use | Server, desktop, Android | Web browsers, Node.js |
| Naming | “Java” is a brand name; not related to “JavaScript” | “JavaScript” is a language name; unrelated to Java |

---

## Ecosystem Highlights

| Category | Popular Tools / Libraries |
|----------|---------------------------|
| **Build** | Maven, Gradle, Ant |
| **Testing** | JUnit, TestNG, Mockito |
| **Dependency Injection** | Spring Framework, CDI (Jakarta EE) |
| **Web** | Spring MVC, Jakarta EE Servlets, Vert.x |
| **Data Access** | JDBC, Hibernate, JPA |
| **Reactive** | Project Reactor, RxJava, Akka |
| **Containerization** | Docker, Kubernetes (Java apps run in containers just like any other language) |

---

## Learning Path

1. **Basics** – Syntax, control flow, OOP fundamentals.  
2. **Core APIs** – Collections, I/O, networking, concurrency.  
3. **Advanced Topics** – Generics, annotations, reflection, streams.  
4. **Frameworks** – Pick one (Spring Boot is a common starting point).  
5. **Build & Deploy** – Maven/Gradle, CI/CD pipelines, Docker.  

---

### Bottom Line

Java is a versatile, mature language that powers everything from enterprise back‑ends and Android apps to embedded devices and big‑data platforms. Its “write once, run anywhere” promise, combined with a vast ecosystem of libraries and tools, makes it a staple in many software development environments.
